rounds.t: SIADH, diabetes insipidus, and primary polydipsia

q.s: A 64-year-old smoker has confusion. Serum Na+ 118 mEq/L, serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ 60 mEq/L. He appears euvolemic. What is the most likely diagnosis?
e: Primary polydipsia produces maximally dilute urine.
He is euvolemic, and hypovolemia would lower urine Na+.
Correct. Euvolemic hyponatremia with urine osm > serum osm and continued urinary Na+ excretion is SIADH; small cell lung cancer is a classic ectopic source.
DI causes hypernatremia and dilute urine.
Cirrhosis causes hypervolemic hyponatremia with low urine Na+.

q.s: In SIADH, why do patients remain clinically euvolemic despite retaining free water?
o: Volume expansion lowers aldosterone and raises ANP/BNP, increasing urinary Na+ excretion
The retained water stays inside cells only
e: Correct. These responses normalize extracellular volume, producing euvolemic hyponatremia.

q.s: What is the first-line treatment for asymptomatic SIADH?
e: Correct. Fluid restriction is first line.
Reserved for severe or symptomatic hyponatremia.
Isotonic saline can worsen hyponatremia in SIADH.

q.s: A patient with refractory SIADH is started on an oral drug that blocks V2 receptors. Which drug is it?
e: A mineralocorticoid, not an ADH antagonist.
Correct. Tolvaptan (and conivaptan) are ADH antagonists used for SIADH.

q.s: Which drug is a recognized cause of SIADH?
e: Demeclocycline treats SIADH and causes nephrogenic DI.
Correct. SSRIs, carbamazepine and cyclophosphamide are drug causes of SIADH.

q.s: The mnemonic "HEELD-up water" lists causes of SIADH. Which is NOT one of them?
o: Ectopic ADH from small cell lung cancer
e: Correct. Hypercalcemia causes nephrogenic DI, not SIADH.

q.s: A 35-year-old woman with schizophrenia drinks 8 L of water daily. Serum Na+ 131 mEq/L, serum osmolality 270 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 80 mOsm/kg. After water restriction, urine osmolality rises to 750 mOsm/kg. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Low serum osmolality with a strong rise in urine osmolality (>700) after water restriction indicates primary polydipsia.
Nephrogenic DI has high serum osmolality and little response.
Central DI has high serum osmolality and little response to water restriction.
SIADH has concentrated urine at baseline.

q.s: A 45-year-old man with bipolar disorder on long-term lithium has polyuria. Water deprivation fails to concentrate his urine, and desmopressin causes minimal change. What is the diagnosis?
e: Not with lithium and desmopressin resistance.
Polydipsia concentrates urine with water restriction.
Correct. Lithium causes ADH resistance; urine osmolality changes little after desmopressin.

q.s: Which electrolyte abnormality can cause nephrogenic DI?
e: Correct. Hypercalcemia and hypokalemia can cause nephrogenic DI.

q.s: A patient with lithium-induced nephrogenic DI needs ongoing lithium. Which diuretic can paradoxically reduce urine output?
e: Correct. Amiloride (and HCTZ) treat nephrogenic DI; amiloride also limits lithium entry into collecting duct cells.

q.s: Which pattern of serum osmolality and ADH fits central DI?
e: Correct. Central DI has low ADH and high serum osmolality.

q.s: A man has polyuria after pituitary surgery limited to the posterior pituitary. The surgeon says the DI may be transient. Why?
o: The anterior pituitary will take over ADH production
The kidneys will become more sensitive to ADH
Hypothalamic ADH can still reach the circulation via portal capillaries in the median eminence
e: The anterior pituitary does not make ADH.
Correct. Damage below the median eminence or in the posterior pituitary may cause only transient DI.

q.s: In a water deprivation test, urine specific gravity in DI or primary polydipsia at baseline is typically:
e: Correct. Both produce large volumes of dilute urine with specific gravity <1.006.

q.s: Which treatment is used for central DI?
A child has polyuria since infancy, hypernatremia and high ADH. A V2 receptor mutation is found. What is the mode of disease?
e: Correct. Hereditary nephrogenic DI is often due to V2 receptor mutation.
ADH is high, so the problem is resistance.

q.s: When is desmopressin given during a water deprivation test?
o: Never; it is a separate test
At the start, before restricting water
When serum osmolality exceeds about 295–300, Na+ reaches 145, or urine osmolality fails to rise
e: It is part of the test.
That indicates primary polydipsia and stops the test.
Correct. These thresholds trigger desmopressin administration.

q.s: Which drug used to treat SIADH can itself cause nephrogenic DI?
e: Not a cause of nephrogenic DI.
Correct. Demeclocycline is an ADH antagonist used for SIADH and a drug cause of nephrogenic DI.
A V2 antagonist; its intended effect is aquaresis, but the classic answer is demeclocycline.

q.s: In SIADH, the relationship between urine and serum osmolality is:
o: Urine osmolality < serum osmolality with low urine Na+
e: Correct. Inappropriately concentrated urine despite low serum osmolality.
That is dilute urine, seen in polydipsia.
That suggests polydipsia or low solute intake.

q.s: Which is a cause of central DI?
o: Infiltrative disease such as Langerhans cell histiocytosis or sarcoidosis
e: Correct. Brain injury, tumors, surgery and infiltrative diseases cause central DI.

q.s: A woman with SIADH and seizures from Na+ 112 mEq/L needs urgent treatment. What is appropriate?
e: Correct. Symptomatic severe hyponatremia is treated with hypertonic saline (corrected slowly).

q.s: A 30-year-old woman had massive postpartum hemorrhage 3 months ago. She could not breastfeed and now has amenorrhea and cold intolerance. What is the diagnosis?
e: Possible postpartum, but the hemorrhage history points to Sheehan.
Asherman causes amenorrhea but not failure to lactate or cold intolerance.
Does not explain failure to lactate and amenorrhea.
Correct. Ischemic pituitary infarction after postpartum hemorrhage causes failure to lactate, amenorrhea and cold intolerance.

q.s: Why is the pituitary vulnerable to infarction in late pregnancy?
o: Prolactin is toxic to the gland
Estrogen causes thrombosis of the portal vessels
The gland enlarges during pregnancy, increasing susceptibility to hypoperfusion
e: Correct. Pregnancy-induced pituitary growth makes it vulnerable.

q.s: Which hormone replacement is most urgent in a patient with new panhypopituitarism?
e: Correct. Glucocorticoids are given first; thyroxine before steroids can precipitate adrenal crisis.
Only needed if posterior pituitary is involved.
Thyroxine first can precipitate adrenal crisis.

q.s: A 10-year-old boy has headaches, bitemporal hemianopia and a calcified suprasellar mass. Which cause of hypopituitarism is most likely?
e: Less likely in a child with calcification.
Correct. Craniopharyngioma is a classic childhood pituitary mass causing hypopituitarism.

q.s: Which of the following is NOT listed as a cause of hypopituitarism?
e: Correct. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism, not hypopituitarism.

q.s: A 48-year-old man notes his rings no longer fit, his voice deepened and he sweats heavily. He has frontal bossing and a large furrowed tongue. What is the best initial test?
e: Correct. ↑ IGF-1 is the best screening test for acromegaly.
GH fluctuates through the day and is unreliable.

q.s: Which test confirms acromegaly?
o: Rise of GH with insulin hypoglycemia
Failure of GH to suppress after an oral glucose tolerance test
Failure of cortisol to suppress with dexamethasone

q.s: What is the most common cause of death in acromegaly?
o: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction from LVH
e: Risk is increased, but not the most common cause.
Correct. HFpEF is the most common cause of death.

q.s: A man with acromegaly has persistent disease after transsphenoidal surgery. Which drug blocks GH receptors directly?
e: A somatostatin analog that lowers GH secretion.
Correct. Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist.
A dopamine agonist that can lower GH.

q.s: What is the first-line treatment for acromegaly due to a pituitary adenoma?
e: Correct. Surgery is first; drugs are used if not cured.

q.s: Which metabolic finding is typical of acromegaly?
o: Impaired glucose tolerance from insulin resistance

q.s: GH excess in a child before epiphyseal fusion causes:
e: A FGFR3 mutation, not GH excess.
Correct. Increased linear growth through unfused epiphyses ("gigantism in juniors").

q.s: Which cardiovascular finding is common in acromegaly?
A woman develops hypopituitarism after postpartum hemorrhage. Which hormones are MAINLY affected?
e: DI can occur, but the anterior gland is mainly affected.
Thyroid failure is secondary to low TSH.
Correct. Sheehan syndrome mainly affects the anterior pituitary.

q.s: Which joint problem is a feature of acromegaly?
Why are random GH levels a poor test for acromegaly?
o: GH is not measurable in serum
GH levels are always normal in acromegaly
GH has a half-life of several days
GH is bound to IGF-1 in serum
GH is secreted in pulses and fluctuates through the day

q.s: A dopamine agonist may be used in acromegaly. Which one?
e: Correct. Dopamine agonists such as cabergoline can lower GH.

q.s: Which facial change is typical of acromegaly?
o: Frontal bossing and coarsening of facial features

q.s: Hormone replacement for hypopituitarism includes all EXCEPT:
e: Correct. Thyroxine is given directly, not TSH.

q.s: A 58-year-old man with acromegaly asks why he sweats so much and his voice has deepened. These features, along with a large furrowed tongue, are caused by:
o: Excess GH acting through IGF-1 on soft tissues
e: Prolactin does not cause these features.
Correct. Diaphoresis, deep voice and macroglossia are classic acromegaly findings.
Hyperthyroidism causes sweating but not macroglossia or deep voice.

rounds.t: Clinical features of hypothyroidism vs hyperthyroidism

q.s: A 52-year-old woman has weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and slow-relaxing ankle reflexes. Which lab pattern is expected if the cause is primary?
e: Correct. Primary hypothyroidism raises TSH and lowers free T4.

q.s: Why does hypothyroidism cause nonpitting edema (myxedema)?
o: Glycosaminoglycans accumulate in interstitial spaces, increasing osmotic pressure and water retention

q.s: A patient with hypothyroidism has hyponatremia. Why?
Which lipid change is expected in hypothyroidism?
A hypothyroid patient has proximal weakness and creatine kinase of 900 U/L. What is the diagnosis?
e: Correct. Hypothyroid myopathy causes proximal weakness with ↑ CK.

q.s: A patient taps a muscle and sees a small lump rise on its surface. This sign, seen in hypothyroidism, is called:
e: Correct. A small lump on muscle when struck with a hammer.

q.s: Which neuropathy is associated with hypothyroidism?
A 28-year-old woman with hyperthyroidism has lid retraction. What causes this?
o: Increased sympathetic stimulation of the superior tarsal muscle

q.s: Why does hyperthyroidism increase fracture risk?
o: T3 stimulates osteoclast differentiation and bone resorption

q.s: A 70-year-old man has new atrial fibrillation and weight loss. TSH is suppressed. Which mechanism explains the cardiac effects of thyroid hormone excess?
o: ↑ number and sensitivity of β-adrenergic receptors, ↑ sarcolemmal ATPase and ↓ phospholamban

q.s: A woman with Graves disease has thickened, raised skin over her shins. What is this?
e: Correct. Pretibial myxedema is seen in Graves disease.

q.s: Which GI finding is typical of hyperthyroidism?
o: Hyperdefecation or diarrhea from increased motility

q.s: A thyrotoxic patient has proximal weakness. CK is likely:
e: Correct. Thyrotoxic myopathy has normal CK.

q.s: Which skin finding suggests hypothyroidism rather than hyperthyroidism?
o: Dry, cool skin with coarse, brittle hair

q.s: Hyperthyroidism raises body heat production mainly through increased synthesis of:
o: Uncoupling protein in the liver only
e: Correct. ↑ Na+/K+-ATPase increases BMR and calorigenesis.

q.s: Which reflex finding is typical of hyperthyroidism?
Which cardiovascular finding is typical of hypothyroidism?
o: Bradycardia with dyspnea on exertion from ↓ cardiac output
Wide pulse pressure with systolic hypertension

q.s: Which lipid change is expected in hyperthyroidism?
Fine tremor in hyperthyroidism is due to:
Which reproductive finding can occur in hyperthyroid men?
A 45-year-old woman has a painless, moderately enlarged thyroid and fatigue. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive. Biopsy shows lymphoid aggregates with germinal centers and Hürthle cells. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Chronic autoimmune thyroiditis with anti-TPO, Hürthle cells and germinal centers.

q.s: A patient with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis develops a rapidly enlarging thyroid. Which malignancy is she at increased risk for?
What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions?
Early in Hashimoto thyroiditis, a patient may be briefly hyperthyroid. Why?
o: Follicular rupture releases stored thyroid hormone ("Hashitoxicosis")

q.s: A 38-year-old woman has fever, jaw pain and an exquisitely tender thyroid 2 weeks after a viral illness. ESR is 95 mm/h. Diagnosis?
e: Possible, but the classic post-viral painful gland with ↑ ESR is de Quervain.
Correct. Painful thyroid after viral infection with ↑ ESR.

q.s: What is the natural history of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis?
A 55-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, rock-hard, fixed, painless thyroid with tracheal compression. He also has retroperitoneal fibrosis. Diagnosis?
e: Mimicked, but the IgG4 association suggests Riedel.
Correct. Invasive fibrous thyroiditis, part of IgG4-related disease.

q.s: Riedel thyroiditis is associated with which disease spectrum?
e: Correct. Includes autoimmune pancreatitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis and aortitis.

q.s: A woman has palpitations 2 months after delivery, followed by fatigue and weight gain at 6 months, then recovers by 1 year. Diagnosis?
e: Would not resolve on its own this way.
Correct. A self-limited Hashimoto variant: hyperthyroid → hypothyroid → euthyroid within a year.

q.s: A newborn has a protuberant tongue, umbilical hernia, puffy face and poor feeding. What is the most common cause of this condition in iodine-sufficient regions?
e: Correct. Thyroid dysgenesis or dyshormonogenesis causes congenital hypothyroidism.

q.s: Which is one of the "6 P's" of congenital hypothyroidism?
e: Correct. Pot-bellied, pale, puffy-faced, protruding umbilicus, protuberant tongue, poor brain development.

q.s: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism worldwide, and how does it typically present?
A patient on long-term amiodarone develops hypothyroidism. Which statement is correct?
o: Amiodarone is a recognized drug cause of hypothyroidism (and thyroiditis)
It is due to increased TBG
The cause is amiodarone's sodium content
e: Correct. Amiodarone and lithium are drug causes.

q.s: A critically ill ICU patient has low T3, normal T4 and normal TSH without thyroid disease. Diagnosis?
e: TSH and T4 would be low.

q.s: Which HLA type is associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis?
Which serology is typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis?
Granulomatous inflammation on thyroid histology suggests:
Riedel thyroiditis is important to distinguish from which malignancy that it can mimic?
e: Correct. Fibrosis extending into local structures mimics anaplastic carcinoma.
Possible, but the stated mimic is anaplastic.

q.s: About what fraction of patients with Riedel thyroiditis are hypothyroid?
Dyshormonogenesis causing congenital hypothyroidism is often due to mutations in:

rounds.t: Hyperthyroidism, thyroid storm, goiter, and adenoma

q.s: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, a diffuse nontender goiter, exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema. What is the mechanism of her disease?
o: Autonomous nodules from TSH receptor mutations
Excess TSH from a pituitary tumor
IgG antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor (type II hypersensitivity)
e: Correct. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin drives Graves disease.

q.s: What is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism?
e: Common in older adults but not most common overall.

q.s: A woman with Graves disease delivers a baby who is tachycardic and irritable with a goiter. What explains this?
o: Maternal thyroid-stimulating IgG crosses the placenta
Maternal T4 crossing in large amounts
e: Correct. TSI can cause transient neonatal hyperthyroidism.
PTU causes fetal hypothyroidism if anything.

q.s: How does Graves orbitopathy cause exophthalmos?
o: Direct T4 toxicity to orbital muscles
T-cell infiltration and cytokines stimulate fibroblasts to secrete hydrophilic GAGs, causing muscle swelling and more orbital fat
e: Lid retraction is separate from true proptosis.

q.s: Graves orbitopathy is treated with:
Graves disease histology shows:
o: Tall, crowded follicular epithelial cells with scalloped colloid

q.s: Graves disease is associated with which HLA types?
A 72-year-old woman has palpitations and a nodular goiter. Radioactive iodine scan shows several hot nodules with suppressed surrounding tissue. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Hyperfunctioning nodules work independently of TSH.

q.s: What is the genetic basis of autonomy in most toxic multinodular goiters?
A man with untreated Graves disease has pneumonia and develops fever 40.5°C, delirium, diarrhea and atrial fibrillation at 170/min. What is the most likely cause of death if untreated?
e: LFTs may rise, but not the main cause.
Correct. Thyroid storm can kill through tachyarrhythmia.

q.s: Which is one of the "4 P's" of thyroid storm treatment?
e: Glucocorticoids are one of the 4 P's, but not as monotherapy.
Correct. β-blockers, PTU, glucocorticoids and potassium iodide.

q.s: In thyroid storm, potassium iodide reduces T4 synthesis through:
e: Correct. An iodide load temporarily turns off TPO.

q.s: Why is propylthiouracil preferred over methimazole in thyroid storm?
o: PTU also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion

q.s: A 24-year-old woman has thyrotoxicosis, a small gland and LOW serum thyroglobulin. She works in a weight-loss clinic. Most likely cause?
o: Exogenous thyrotoxicosis from taking thyroid hormone
e: Correct. Suspect in patients trying to lose weight; thyroglobulin is suppressed.

q.s: A patient with a nodular goiter becomes hyperthyroid after iodinated contrast. What is this called?
A woman has hyperthyroidism, an ovarian mass and a nonenlarged thyroid. What is the likely source?
o: Struma ovarii (thyroid tissue in a teratoma)
e: Possible, but the listed ectopic thyroid source is struma ovarii.

q.s: Which condition causes a SMOOTH, diffuse goiter?
e: Correct. Graves, Hashimoto, iodine deficiency and TSH-secreting adenoma cause diffuse goiter.

q.s: A solitary thyroid nodule is "cold" on radioactive iodine scan. Biopsy shows a follicular lesion without capsular or vascular invasion. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. No capsular or vascular invasion distinguishes adenoma from carcinoma.

q.s: Most thyroid adenomas appear how on radioactive iodine scanning?
Which nodule finding on radioactive iodine scan is LEAST likely to be malignant?
e: Cold nodules have higher malignancy risk.
Correct. Hyperfunctioning (hot) nodules are rarely malignant.

q.s: A 35-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule and a palpable cervical lymph node. FNA shows cells with empty-appearing nuclei, nuclear grooves and psammoma bodies. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. "Orphan Annie" nuclei, grooves and psammoma bodies; most common type with nodal spread.

q.s: Which risk factor is most associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma?
e: Correct. Also RET/PTC rearrangements and BRAF mutations.

q.s: Which mutation is associated with papillary thyroid carcinoma?
A 50-year-old woman has a thyroid mass and a pathologic fracture of the femur from a bone metastasis. Thyroid histology shows uniform follicles invading the capsule and vessels. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Invades capsule and vasculature with common hematogenous spread.

q.s: Why can fine-needle aspiration NOT distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma?
o: Both have identical nuclear features and carcinoma is defined by capsular or vascular invasion seen only on full histology

q.s: Follicular thyroid carcinoma is associated with which genetic changes?

A 30-year-old man has a thyroid nodule, elevated calcitonin and hypertension with episodic headaches. His father had a similar thyroid cancer. Biopsy shows polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma. Which gene is mutated?
e: Associated with pheochromocytoma but not medullary carcinoma.
Correct. Medullary thyroid carcinoma with MEN 2A/2B is due to RET mutations.

q.s: The amyloid in medullary thyroid carcinoma stains with:
A 78-year-old man has a rapidly enlarging neck mass, hoarseness, dyspnea and dysphagia. Histology shows pleomorphic cells with frequent mitoses. Prognosis?
e: Anaplastic tumors do not take up iodine well.
Correct. Anaplastic carcinoma has a very poor prognosis.

q.s: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma most often arises from:
o: Dedifferentiation of a preexisting follicular or papillary carcinoma

q.s: What is the most common type of thyroid cancer?
After thyroidectomy, a patient has perioral numbness and carpal spasm on day 1. What is the most likely cause?
o: Hypocalcemia from removal or injury of parathyroid glands

q.s: After thyroidectomy, a patient has hoarseness and dysphagia. Which nerve was injured, and during ligation of which vessel?
o: External laryngeal nerve; superior thyroid artery
Recurrent laryngeal nerve; inferior thyroid artery

q.s: A professional singer cannot reach high notes after thyroid surgery but has a normal speaking voice. Which nerve was most likely injured?
o: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
e: Correct. Injured during ligation of the superior thyroid pedicle; supplies the cricothyroid muscle.

q.s: Prophylactic thyroidectomy is recommended for carriers of which mutation?
e: Correct. Medullary carcinoma risk is very high.

q.s: Which tumor marker is used to monitor medullary thyroid carcinoma?
e: Used for papillary and follicular carcinoma.

q.s: Thyroid nodules are typically diagnosed by:
Papillary thyroid carcinoma generally has which prognosis?
e: Correct. Despite frequent lymph node spread, prognosis is good.

q.s: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from which cells?
Which thyroid cancer spreads mainly by the bloodstream to bone and lung?
e: Can spread both ways but classic hematogenous answer is follicular.

q.s: A 55-year-old woman has kidney stones, constipation, depression and bone pain. Calcium 11.8 mg/dL, phosphate low, PTH elevated. What is the most likely cause?
e: Calcium would be low or normal.
Correct. 1° hyperparathyroidism, usually an adenoma: "stones, thrones, bones, groans, psychiatric overtones."
Usually urine calcium is low and stones uncommon.

q.s: Bone biopsy in severe hyperparathyroidism shows cystic spaces filled with brown fibrous tissue containing osteoclasts and hemosiderin. What is this called?
A 60-year-old man on dialysis has hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, ↑ ALP and ↑ PTH. What is the diagnosis?
o: Secondary hyperparathyroidism from chronic kidney disease
e: Correct. CKD causes hypovitaminosis D and hyperphosphatemia, lowering calcium.

q.s: Years later, the same dialysis patient develops hypercalcemia with very high PTH that persists after correcting phosphate and vitamin D. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Autonomous PTH secretion after long-standing ESRD.

q.s: Phosphate level distinguishes secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD from most other causes. In CKD it is:
e: Most other causes of hyperparathyroidism have low phosphate.
The key point is that it is high.

q.s: A 40-year-old man has mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH and a 24-hour urine calcium that is very low. His mother has the same findings. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Defective Ca2+-sensing receptors cause mild hypercalcemia with hypocalciuria.

q.s: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is caused by:
Two days after thyroidectomy, a woman has hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia. Tapping in front of her ear causes facial twitching. What is the name of this sign?
e: Correct. Tap the cheek: facial contraction.
Carpal spasm with a BP cuff.

q.s: Inflating a BP cuff above systolic pressure for 3 minutes causes carpal spasm. This is:
A child has short stature, round face and shortened 4th and 5th metacarpals. Labs: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. End-organ resistance to PTH from a maternally transmitted GNAS mutation with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy.

q.s: A child has the physical features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy but normal calcium, phosphate and PTH. The mutation was inherited from the father. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Paternally transmitted GNAS mutation without end-organ resistance.

q.s: The GNAS gene mutated in pseudohypoparathyroidism encodes:
e: Correct. Loss of Gsα blocks adenylate cyclase activation by PTH.

q.s: Why does the inheritance parent matter in GNAS disorders?
o: GNAS is imprinted; in the kidney the maternal allele is the one expressed
GNAS is on the Y chromosome
Only fathers can pass it on
e: Correct. Maternal mutation causes PTH resistance; paternal mutation does not.

q.s: Which pattern fits vitamin D deficiency?
o: Normal or ↓ Ca2+ and phosphate, ↑ PTH, ↑ ALP, ↓ 25(OH)D

q.s: Which pattern fits hypoparathyroidism?
A newborn with a cardiac outflow defect and absent thymic shadow has seizures from hypocalcemia. Why?
e: A possible cause of neonatal hypocalcemia, but the syndrome points to DiGeorge.

q.s: Which finding is typical of primary hyperparathyroidism?
Renal disease leading to secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism and bone lesions is called:
A patient with hypercalcemia has suppressed PTH. Which is the most likely category?
o: PTH-independent hypercalcemia (malignancy, excess vitamin D or calcium intake)

q.s: Which acute GI complication can primary hyperparathyroidism cause?

rounds.t: Diabetes mellitus, DKA, HHS, and hypoglycemia

q.s: A 12-year-old boy has polyuria, weight loss, vomiting and deep rapid breathing. Glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.12, HCO3− 8 mEq/L, serum ketones positive. Which ketone body predominates in the blood?
In the same patient, serum potassium is 5.6 mEq/L. Which statement about total body potassium is correct?
o: K+ should be withheld throughout treatment
Total body K+ is depleted despite normal or high serum K+
e: Serum K+ is high but stores are depleted.
K+ is given to replete stores once levels allow.
Correct. Insulin lack and acidosis shift K+ out of cells; osmotic diuresis loses K+ in urine.

q.s: A 78-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes in a nursing home is lethargic. Glucose 980 mg/dL, serum osmolality 360 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38, no ketones. Diagnosis?
e: Ketones and acidosis would be present.
Correct. Profound hyperglycemia, high osmolality, normal pH and no ketones.

q.s: Why do patients in HHS usually lack ketoacidosis?
o: They have enough insulin to suppress lipolysis and ketogenesis
They have no insulin at all

q.s: A patient with DKA develops black necrotic eschar in the nasal cavity and facial swelling. What life-threatening complication is this?
e: A DKA complication, but not this picture.
Possible but mucormycosis is the classic DKA infection.

q.s: What is the initial treatment of DKA?
o: IV fluids, IV insulin and potassium, adding glucose as glucose falls

q.s: Which HLA types are associated with type 1 diabetes?
Which statement about genetic predisposition in diabetes is correct?
o: Type 1 has 90% concordance in identical twins
Type 2 has stronger genetic predisposition, about 90% twin concordance

q.s: Islet histology in long-standing type 2 diabetes characteristically shows:
Which autoantibody supports a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes?
e: Correct. Antibodies to islet cell cytoplasm, GAD65 and insulin may be present.

q.s: Which test result diagnoses diabetes mellitus?
A patient with sickle cell disease has an HbA1c of 5.4% despite fasting glucose of 160 mg/dL. Why might HbA1c be misleading?
o: HbA1c is influenced by RBC turnover
e: Correct. Shortened RBC survival lowers HbA1c.

q.s: Diabetic retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy from small vessel disease are mainly due to:
What is the most common cause of death in patients with diabetes?
Diabetic cataracts and neuropathy partly result from sorbitol accumulation. Which enzyme combination leads to this?
o: Aldose reductase present with low or absent sorbitol dehydrogenase
High sorbitol dehydrogenase, low aldose reductase

q.s: A patient with long-standing diabetes has early satiety, vomiting of undigested food and bloating. Which complication is this?
A 66-year-old man on glyburide skips lunch and is found confused and sweaty. He takes propranolol and had no warning symptoms on prior episodes. Why?
o: β-blockers blunt neurogenic warning symptoms (hypoglycemia unawareness)

q.s: Which symptom is NEUROGLYCOPENIC rather than neurogenic?
e: Correct. Altered mental status and seizures reflect CNS glucose lack.

q.s: An unconscious patient with diabetes has glucose 35 mg/dL and no IV access. What should be given?
e: Used for sulfonylurea overdose but not first here.

q.s: Which condition can cause diabetes through unopposed counter-regulatory hormones?
o: Excess GH or epinephrine, or glucocorticoid therapy

rounds.t: Cushing syndrome, adrenal insufficiency, and hyperaldosteronism

q.s: What is the most common cause of Cushing syndrome?
o: Ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer
e: Correct. Causes ↓ ACTH and bilateral adrenal atrophy.

q.s: A 40-year-old woman has truncal obesity, purple striae, hypertension and hyperglycemia. Low-dose dexamethasone fails to suppress cortisol. ACTH is elevated. High-dose dexamethasone suppresses cortisol. Next step?
o: CT of the chest for ectopic ACTH
e: ACTH is high, so not adrenal.
Ectopic sources usually do not suppress with high-dose.
Correct. ACTH-dependent with suppression on high-dose dexamethasone suggests Cushing disease.

q.s: A 62-year-old smoker has hypertension, hypokalemia, hyperpigmentation and very high ACTH that does not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone. Most likely cause?
o: Ectopic ACTH secretion (eg, small cell lung cancer)

q.s: Which screening test is used for Cushing syndrome?
o: 24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol or 1 mg overnight dexamethasone test

q.s: A patient with Cushing syndrome has suppressed ACTH and a unilateral adrenal mass. What happens to the contralateral adrenal?
e: Correct. Low ACTH causes atrophy of the uninvolved gland.

q.s: Which finding is part of "MOON FACIES" in Cushing syndrome?
e: Correct. Also metabolic syndrome, obesity, neuropsychiatric symptoms, facial plethora, androgen excess, cataract, immunosuppression, ecchymoses, skin changes.

q.s: A 35-year-old woman has fatigue, salt craving, orthostatic hypotension and darkened buccal mucosa. Na+ 128, K+ 5.9 mEq/L. What is the diagnosis?
e: Correct. ↓ cortisol and ↓ aldosterone with hyperpigmentation from ↑ MSH.

q.s: Why does secondary adrenal insufficiency NOT cause hyperkalemia?
o: Aldosterone synthesis is preserved because the RAAS and adrenal gland are intact

q.s: What is the most common cause of Addison disease in high-income countries?
What is the most common cause of tertiary adrenal insufficiency?
o: Abrupt cessation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy

q.s: A 19-year-old college student has fever, petechial rash and shock. Autopsy shows bilateral adrenal hemorrhage. Which organism and syndrome?
A patient on long-term prednisone has surgery and develops hypotension, abdominal pain and confusion. What is the likely cause?
e: Possible, but the steroid history suggests adrenal crisis.
Correct. Stress increases glucocorticoid needs in suppressed patients.

q.s: In suspected adrenal insufficiency with a low AM cortisol, a HIGH ACTH indicates:
e: ACTH would be low or inappropriately normal.

q.s: Which metabolic disturbance is typical of primary adrenal insufficiency?
A 45-year-old man has resistant hypertension, K+ 3.0 mEq/L and metabolic alkalosis. Aldosterone is high and renin is low. What is the diagnosis?
o: Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome or bilateral hyperplasia)

q.s: A woman with renal artery stenosis has hypertension and hypokalemia. What renin and aldosterone pattern is expected?
Why does primary hyperaldosteronism not cause edema?
o: The aldosterone escape mechanism increases sodium excretion

q.s: Which condition is a cause of SECONDARY hyperaldosteronism?
e: Correct. Also cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renovascular hypertension and renin-secreting tumors.

q.s: Cushing disease is responsible for what share of endogenous Cushing syndrome?
A patient with primary adrenal insufficiency is started on hydrocortisone. Which additional drug is usually needed?
e: Correct. Primary disease loses aldosterone too; treatment is glucocorticoid ± mineralocorticoid.

rounds.t: Neuroendocrine tumors, pheochromocytoma, MEN, and islet tumors

q.s: A 2-year-old has a firm, irregular abdominal mass crossing the midline and random eye movements with jerking limbs. Urine HVA and VMA are elevated. Diagnosis?
e: Smooth, unilateral, not crossing the midline.
Correct. Opsoclonus-myoclonus ("dancing eyes, dancing feet") with ↑ HVA/VMA.

q.s: Which oncogene amplification is associated with neuroblastoma?
Which histologic finding is characteristic of neuroblastoma?
e: Correct. Neuroblasts around a central area of neuropil.

q.s: A 38-year-old woman has episodic headaches, sweating, palpitations and BP 220/120 mm Hg during spells. Plasma metanephrines are high and CT shows an adrenal mass. What must be given BEFORE a β-blocker?
o: An irreversible α-antagonist such as phenoxybenzamine
e: Correct. α-blockade first avoids hypertensive crisis ("A before B").

q.s: Which is part of the "rule of 10's" for pheochromocytoma?
e: Correct. Also 10% malignant, extra-adrenal, calcify and in kids.

q.s: Pheochromocytoma can cause polycythemia by secreting:
Which germline syndrome is associated with pheochromocytoma?
A man has hyperparathyroidism, recurrent duodenal ulcers and a prolactinoma. Which gene is mutated?
e: Correct. MEN1: parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas (3 P's).

q.s: A 25-year-old man with a marfanoid habitus has bumpy lips and tongue, medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma. Which syndrome?
e: Has parathyroid hyperplasia, no mucosal neuromas.
Correct. Medullary carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas and marfanoid habitus.

q.s: Which component distinguishes MEN2A from MEN2B?
e: Correct. MEN2A has parathyroid hyperplasia; MEN2B has mucosal neuromas instead.

q.s: What is the inheritance pattern of all MEN syndromes?
A 40-year-old woman has confusion and diplopia before breakfast that resolve after eating. Glucose 38 mg/dL, insulin high, C-peptide high, sulfonylurea screen negative. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Whipple triad with ↑ insulin and ↑ C-peptide.

q.s: Which is one of the "6 D's" of glucagonoma?
e: Correct. Also diabetes, DVT, declining weight, depression, diarrhea.

q.s: A patient has new diabetes, steatorrhea, gallstones and achlorhydria. A pancreatic δ-cell tumor is found. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. Somatostatin inhibits secretin, CCK, gastrin, insulin and glucagon.

q.s: A man with a small bowel carcinoid tumor and liver metastases has flushing, diarrhea and wheezing. Which valve lesion is most likely?
e: Left-sided valves are spared because lung MAO degrades serotonin.
Correct. Carcinoid syndrome causes right-sided lesions (tricuspid regurgitation, pulmonic stenosis).

q.s: Why does carcinoid syndrome usually require liver metastases when the primary tumor is in the intestine?
o: Serotonin from gut tumors undergoes hepatic first-pass metabolism; metastases release it directly into systemic circulation

q.s: A patient with carcinoid syndrome develops dermatitis, diarrhea and dementia. Which deficiency explains this?
e: Correct. Excess serotonin synthesis consumes tryptophan.

q.s: Which test diagnoses carcinoid syndrome?
A patient has refractory duodenal and jejunal ulcers and diarrhea. Gastrin rises paradoxically after secretin injection. Diagnosis?
e: Correct. A positive secretin stimulation test.
Causes high gastrin but no ulcers.

q.s: Neuroendocrine tumors share which immunohistochemical markers?
o: Chromogranin A, synaptophysin and neuron-specific enolase
